example_01.category: Unnecessary RBAC permissions for authenticated users
example_01.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, delete, and watch permissions on pods in the webapp namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can manage all pods in the webapp namespace. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous verbs being granted, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being bound.

example_02.category: Overly broad RBAC permissions to authenticated users for monitoring and management purposes
example_02.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all resources in the cluster (pods, nodes, services, endpoints, namespaces) via the apiGroups: [""] scope. The rolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can access all these resources without needing a specific resource or namespace label. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together — the clusterrole alone does not reveal the dangerous permissions being granted, and the binding file alone does not restrict them to just authenticated users.

example_03.category: Unnecessary service account access for unauthenticated users
example_03.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, and patch permissions on deployments and services in the cicd namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:unauthenticated, meaning any unauthenticated user can access all resources within the cicd namespace. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not restrict access to unauthenticated users.

example_04.category: Unnecessary secret access for database management
example_04.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the database namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can now read all secrets in the database namespace. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_05.category: Overly broad cluster-level RBAC to unauthenticated users
example_05.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on nodes and nodes/status as well as persistent volumes. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to system:unauthenticated, meaning any unauthenticated user — with no credentials at all — can access these resources in the entire namespace. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subjects, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_06.category: Unnecessary RBAC permissions for authenticated users on sensitive resources
example_06.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on configmaps and pods in the logging namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can access all resources within the logging namespace. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous verbs being granted, and the binding file alone does not restrict them to a specific resource or namespace.

example_07.category: Overly broad cluster role binding to authenticated users
example_07.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, create, update, and patch permissions on serviceaccounts and namespaces. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the system:authenticated group, meaning any authenticated user can perform all these actions across the entire cluster. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_08.category: Unnecessary pod execution and log access for unauthenticated users
example_08.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on pods. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:unauthenticated, meaning any unauthenticated user — with no credentials at all — can execute pods and view their logs in the development namespace. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_09.category: Insecure network policy for unauthenticated access to services and endpoints
example_09.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on all ingresses and services/endpoints in the ingress-nginx namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can access these resources without needing a service account or specific resource permissions. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together — the role alone does not reveal the dangerous verbs being granted, and the binding file alone does not restrict access based on authentication status.

example_10.category: Overly broad cluster-level RBAC granting access to all resources and verbs across multiple API groups, including sensitive ones like secrets and service accounts.
example_10.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, watch, create, update, patch, delete permissions on a wide range of Kubernetes resources (pods, services, configmaps, secrets, serviceaccounts, persistentvolumeclaims) and APIs (apps, networking.k8s.io). This includes sensitive operations like creating and updating deployments, which could be used for unauthorized access to the cluster. The rolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to system:authenticated, allowing any authenticated user to perform all these actions across the entire namespace. The misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together — the role alone does not reveal the dangerous permissions being granted, and the binding file alone does not show the sensitive resources being accessed.

example_11.category: Unnecessary RBAC permissions for a static workload
example_11.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a web application running Nginx and explicitly states it requires no specific access beyond basic pod management. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, watch, create, delete permissions on pods and deployments in the webapp namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the webapp-nginx-sa ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading all three files together: the workload has no legitimate need for these permissions, while the RBAC bindings grant them unnecessarily.

example_12.category: Unnecessary role and rolebinding granting broad access to all resources in the caching namespace, including pods, deployments, and configmaps.
example_12.justification: The deployment.yaml specifies that it is for a Redis cache workload. The role.yaml grants broad access to all resources in the caching namespace, including pods, deployments, and configmaps. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the redis-cache-sa ServiceAccount, which mounts the deployment and pod templates of the Redis cache workload. This misconfiguration only becomes apparent by reading all four files together: the service account is mounted with a workload that has no legitimate need for broad access, while the role and binding grant it exactly that.

example_13.category: Unnecessary role and binding granting access to all resources in the monitoring namespace, including pods, services, endpoints, deployments, and secrets.
example_13.justification: The deployment.yaml specifies that it runs a Prometheus instance on port 9090. The role.yaml grants access to all resources in the monitoring namespace, including pods, services, endpoints, deployments, and secrets. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the prometheus-scraper-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. This misconfiguration allows any user with access to the prometheus-scraper-sa ServiceAccount to perform actions on all resources in the monitoring namespace, including accessing sensitive data like Kubernetes API tokens and secrets. The misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading all four files together.

example_14.category: Unnecessary RBAC permissions on services and endpoints
example_14.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a static file server workload running nginx:1.25 with specific resource requests and limits. The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, delete permissions on services and endpoints in the fileserver namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the fileserver-sa ServiceAccount within the same namespace. Reading all four files together reveals that these permissions are unnecessary for a static web server workload, as it only needs read access to its own service account's resources (which is already provided by the serviceaccount). This misconfiguration allows any user with RBAC permissions on services and endpoints in the fileserver namespace to potentially perform unauthorized actions.

example_15.category: Unnecessary role and rolebinding granting access to all pods in the database namespace, including those that do not belong to any deployment or service account.
example_15.justification: The deployment.yaml specifies a PostgreSQL database workload running postgres:15 with specific environment variables. The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on all pods in the database namespace, including those that do not belong to any deployment or service account. Similarly, the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the postgres-sa ServiceAccount within the database namespace only. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading all four files together: the workload needs access to specific resources (the PostgreSQL image and environment variables), but the role and binding grant permissions on all pods in the entire namespace without any scope or restriction.

example_16.category: Unnecessary RBAC permissions for a workload that does not require them
example_16.justification: The deployment.yaml defines the frontend-react workload running Node.js on port 3000. The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on services and endpoints in the frontend namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to ServiceAccount frontend-react-sa within the same namespace. However, the workload does not require any of these permissions — it only needs read access to its own service account for authentication purposes. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading all three files together: the deployment establishes that no legitimate need exists for these permissions, while the role and binding grant them anyway.

example_17.category: Unnecessary RBAC permissions on services and pods
example_17.justification: The deployment.yaml specifies that the nginx proxy workload runs in a namespace called 'proxy'. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, watch, create, delete permissions on pods and services within this namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds these roles to the ServiceAccount named 'nginx-proxy-sa', which is mounted by the deployment. This misconfiguration allows any user with access to the service account to perform actions that could potentially expose sensitive information or disrupt the intended use of the workload, without needing specific permissions on pods and services themselves. The misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading all four files together.

example_18.category: Unnecessary role and binding granting access to all resources in the logging namespace, including persistent volume claims for storage management.
example_18.justification: The deployment.yaml specifies that it requires access to pods and persistent volume claims. The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, delete permissions on all resources in the logging namespace, including persistent volume claims for storage management. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the elasticsearch-sa ServiceAccount within the logging namespace only. Reading these files together reveals that the workload (elasticsearch) needs access to pods and persistent volume claims but is granted full control over them without any specific need or restriction. This misconfiguration allows unauthorized users to manage storage resources, which could lead to data exposure or misuse.

example_19.category: Unnecessary RBAC permissions for RabbitMQ management tools
example_19.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a RabbitMQ service and its annotations specify it requires access to the rabbitmq-management secrets for management purposes. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, watch, create, and delete permissions on pods and services in the messaging namespace, including creating new deployments via the 'update' verb. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the rabbitmq-sa ServiceAccount within the messaging namespace only. The misconfiguration is only visible by reading all three files together — the deployment establishes that RabbitMQ management tools need access to these secrets for their intended purpose, while the role and binding grant exactly those permissions.

example_20.category: Unnecessary RBAC permissions for a workload that does not require them, and overly broad role binding to an unprivileged service account
example_20.justification: The deployment.yaml defines the nginx-exporter workload running Nginx Prometheus Exporter. The role.yaml grants get, list, watch, update, patch, and delete permissions on deployments, pods, and services in the exports namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the ServiceAccount nginx-exporter-sa within the same namespace, which is unprivileged. This misconfiguration only becomes apparent by reading all four files together: the workload does not need these permissions, but they are granted to an unprivileged service account, leading to unnecessary risk.

example_21.category: Insecure Network Policy for a sensitive service
example_21.justification: The deployment.yaml specifies that the frontend workload runs Nginx and requires access to port 80. The network policy.yaml restricts traffic from pods labeled 'role: ingress-controller' but does not specify any specific ports or services, making it overly broad and potentially insecure for a sensitive service like an HTTP server.

example_22.category: Inadequate network policy for database isolation
example_22.justification: The deployment.yaml specifies that the pod should be isolated from other pods in the same namespace, which is a common requirement for databases. However, the networkpolicy.yaml does not enforce any specific isolation rules between the postgres and backend-api pods. This means that traffic can still flow between them without being restricted by the policy, potentially exposing the database to unauthorized access or attacks. The misconfiguration only becomes apparent when both files are read together.

example_23.category: Insecure network policy for prometheus-scraper traffic
example_23.justification: The deployment.yaml specifies that the Prometheus service runs on port 9090. The networkpolicy.yaml allows ingress traffic from pods labeled 'role: metrics-consumer' to access this port, which is insecure for prometheus-scraper traffic. This misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading both files together — the podSelector in the deployment file does not restrict the allowed traffic, and the policy type specifies that it should allow ingress traffic.

example_24.category: Insecure network policy for a production environment
example_24.justification: The deployment.yaml specifies that the payment-api workload runs on node:20-alpine and uses a podSelector matching labels 'app: payment-api' and 'env: production'. The networkpolicy.yaml allows ingress from pods with selector 'podSelector.matchLabels.role: api-gateway', which is not appropriate for a production environment. This misconfiguration only becomes apparent when the deployment's workload is running on an API gateway, as it opens up access to all pods in the payments namespace that match the 'role' label.

example_25.category: Insecure Network Policy for Elasticsearch with Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
example_25.justification: The deployment.yaml specifies that the Elasticsearch pod should be isolated from other pods in the logging namespace. However, the network policy defined in networkpolicy.yaml allows traffic to all pods matching the role selector 'role: log-shipper'. This means any pod with a label of 'role: log-shipper' can communicate with the Elasticsearch pod, potentially exposing it to unauthorized access or misconfiguration. The misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together — the network policy alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_26.category: Insecure network policy for RabbitMQ, allowing pods from any role to access it externally
example_26.justification: The deployment.yaml specifies that the RabbitMQ pod is running in a namespace called 'messaging'. The networkpolicy.yaml allows all pods with the label 'app: worker' to access the RabbitMQ pod, which is not restricted by any specific role or service account. This policy is insecure because it exposes the RabbitMQ service externally without proper isolation and security measures.

example_27.category: Insecure Network Policy for Jenkins Controller Pods
example_27.justification: The network policy in the deployment.yaml file allows traffic from pods with labels 'role: build-agent' to any pod. This is a security risk because it exposes Jenkins Controller pods to potential attacks, such as port scanning or unauthorized access attempts. The misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading both files together — the deployment establishes that Jenkins Controller pods need no network isolation, while the policy file grants unrestricted traffic from build-agent pods.

example_28.category: Insecure Network Policy for a sensitive workload
example_28.justification: The deployment.yaml specifies that the react-app workload runs on port 3000 and uses an image of node:20-alpine. The network policy.yaml restricts traffic to pods with labels 'role: ingress-controller', which includes the ingress controller itself, potentially allowing unauthenticated access to sensitive ports like 3000. This misconfiguration is only apparent when reading both files together — the deployment establishes a specific port and image for the workload, while the network policy binds it to an ingress controller that could expose any number of services.

example_29.category: Insecure Network Policy for Load Balancer Access
example_29.justification: The deployment.yaml specifies that the API Gateway workload runs on port 80 and 443. The network policy.yaml restricts traffic from pods labeled 'load-balancer' to access the backend service, but it does not specify any restrictions for pods labeled 'api-gateway'. This results in a potential security risk where load balancers could potentially connect directly to the API Gateway without proper authentication or authorization, leading to unauthorized access. The misconfiguration is only apparent when reading both files together.

example_30.category: Inadequate network policy for isolation, allowing pods from a different role to access the worker deployment's resources
example_30.justification: The networkpolicy.yaml allows ingress and egress traffic between pods in the staging namespace. This is problematic because it enables pods with the app: job-scheduler label (which matches the podSelector of the worker deployment) to access resources on the worker deployment, which could potentially expose sensitive information or cause unintended side effects. The misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading both files together — the network policy alone does not reveal the dangerous traffic patterns.

example_31.category: Overly broad ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding granting access to all resources, including non-resource URLs
example_31.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch permissions on all resources in the rbac.authorization.k8s.io API group. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to a ServiceAccount named cicd-deploy-sa within the cicd namespace. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous verbs being granted, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being bound.

example_32.category: Overly broad RBAC permissions for a service account with elevated privileges
example_32.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, and escalate access to roles in the monitoring namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the prometheus-sa ServiceAccount within the monitoring namespace, which is a service account with elevated privileges (elevated because it's part of the monitoring namespace). This misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_33.category: Overly broad impersonation scope for a sensitive role
example_33.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants impersonate permissions on users and serviceaccounts. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the api-gateway-sa ServiceAccount in the webapp namespace, which is not a sensitive role or resource that would typically require such broad impersonation scope. This misconfiguration only becomes apparent by reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_34.category: Unnecessary RBAC permissions for automation users in the devops namespace
example_34.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, delete permissions on deployments and replicasets, as well as pods, services, and configmaps. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to a User named devops-automation-user in the rbac.authorization.k8s.io group within the devops namespace. This means any user with access to the RBAC API can perform these actions across all resources in the devops namespace without needing to authenticate or be part of the devops team. The misconfiguration is only apparent by reading all three files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous permissions, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive scope.

example_35.category: ClusterRole with overly broad permissions to all resources and non-resource URLs, potentially exposing sensitive information or unauthorized access
example_35.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all resources and non-resource URLs in the cluster. The rolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to a security-team group, which means any user or service account within the cluster can access these broad permissions without needing specific roles. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together: the role alone does not reveal the dangerous permissions being granted, and the binding file alone does not restrict them to the intended use case.

example_36.category: Overly broad impersonation scope for a privileged role
example_36.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants impersonate and get permissions on serviceaccounts. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the ServiceAccount workflow-engine-sa in the platform namespace, which is not a privileged role but rather an administrative one (cluster-admin). This misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading both files together: the impersonation scope is too broad for a non-privileged role, and it applies to all serviceaccounts within the platform namespace. The misconfiguration is easily overlooked if only looking at individual manifest files.

example_37.category: Overly broad ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding granting admin access to all resources in the platform namespace, including unauthenticated users.
example_37.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, watch, bind, escalate permissions on roles, clusterroles, and rolebindings. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the platform-automation-sa ServiceAccount in the platform namespace only. However, reading all three files together reveals that the ClusterRole is also granting unauthenticated users access to all resources (including non-resource URLs) via the nonResourceURLs scoping. This misconfiguration allows any user with a valid token or API key to perform administrative actions on all resources within the platform namespace without needing authentication.

example_38.category: Overly broad impersonation to system:masters group
example_38.justification: The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds the infra-group-impersonator ClusterRole to the infra-automation-user, which is a user in the system:masters Group. This means any user with this role can impersonate any member of the system:masters group — including other users and services that do not belong to the system:masters group. The misconfiguration only becomes apparent by reading both files together: the clusterrolefile alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_39.category: Overly broad ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding granting access to all resources in the cluster, including sensitive operations like creating and deleting pods.
example_39.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, delete permissions on all resources in the cluster. The rolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to a Group named platform-engineers, which means any user or service account within that group can perform these operations across the entire cluster. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together: the role alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted, and the binding file alone does not restrict access to specific resources.

example_40.category: Overly broad ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding granting access to all resources, including service accounts and users.
example_40.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, escalate, impersonate, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on all resources. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the tenant-provisioner-sa ServiceAccount in the tenants namespace only. Reading these files together reveals that the role is overly broad — it allows access to all resources without any specific scope or restrictions. This misconfiguration can lead to unintended consequences, such as unauthorized access to sensitive data or services.

example_41.category: Unnecessary secret access for a static website
example_41.justification: The deployment.yaml defines the webapp-nginx workload running nginx:1.25 and explicitly states it serves a static site with no backend API calls or credential access required. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the webapp namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the webapp-nginx-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading all four files together: the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding grant it exactly that.

example_42.category: Unnecessary secret access for Prometheus Node Exporter
example_42.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a node-exporter workload running prom/node-exporter:v1.6.0 and explicitly states in its annotation that it requires access to the monitoring secret for Prometheus Node Exporter's configuration. The role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the monitoring namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the node-exporter-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. Reading all four files together confirms that the workload legitimately needs access to the monitoring secret for Prometheus Node Exporter's configuration, but the permissions are unnecessarily broad due to the binding of a service account with no specific need for secrets.

example_43.category: Unnecessary secret access for monitoring tool
example_43.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a blackbox-exporter workload running prom/blackbox-exporter:0.24.0 and explicitly states in its annotation that it requires access to the probing-credentials secret for monitoring purposes. The role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the probing namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the blackbox-exporter-sa ServiceAccount within the probing namespace only. However, reading all four files together reveals that the workload legitimately needs access to the probing-credentials secret for monitoring, while the role and binding grant it access to all secrets in the probing namespace. This misconfiguration is only apparent when considering the entire cluster configuration.

example_44.category: Unnecessary secret access for a workload that does not require it
example_44.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a memcached workload running memcached:1.6 and explicitly states in its annotation that it requires no credentials or secrets. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the caching namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the memcached-sa ServiceAccount within the same namespace. The workload does not need access to any secrets, but the misconfiguration is only visible by reading all three files together — the deployment establishes that no credentials are needed, while the role and binding grant exactly that.

example_45.category: Unnecessary secret access for Prometheus monitoring
example_45.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a StatsD exporter workload running prom/statsd-exporter:v0.26.0 and explicitly states in its annotation that it requires access to the metrics-credentials secret for Prometheus monitoring purposes. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the metrics namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the prometheus-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible when reading all four files together — the workload needs access to a specific secret for Prometheus monitoring, while the role and binding grant it access to all secrets in the metrics namespace.

example_46.category: Unnecessary secret access for static web server
example_46.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a caddy-frontend workload running the image caddy:2.7 and explicitly states in its annotation that it requires access to secrets for static web server configuration, but the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the frontend namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the caddy-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible when reading all four files together — the workload needs access to specific secrets for its static web server configuration, while the role and binding grant it permissions on all secrets in the frontend namespace.

example_47.category: Unnecessary secret access for a workload that does not require it
example_47.justification: The deployment.yaml defines the Graphite exporter workload running prom/graphite-exporter:0.13.3 and explicitly states in its annotation that it requires access to a secret for Graphite metrics collection, but the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the redis namespace, including the one required by the workload. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the redis-exporter-sa ServiceAccount which is mounted by the deployment. This misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading all four files together: the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding grant it exactly that.

example_48.category: Unnecessary secret access for a workload that does not require it
example_48.justification: The deployment.yaml defines the healthcheck workload running curl images and explicitly states in its annotation that it requires no credentials or secrets. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the staging namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the service account mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_49.category: Unnecessary secret access for web server
example_49.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a web server (httpd:2.4) running in the docs namespace and explicitly states it requires access to secrets for its operation. The role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the docs namespace, while the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the httpd-sa ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. This misconfiguration is only apparent when reading all four files together: the web server has no legitimate need for secret access, but the role and binding grant it exactly that.

example_50.category: Unnecessary secret access for a workload that does not require it
example_50.justification: The deployment.yaml defines the whoami workload running traefik/whoami:v1.10 and explicitly states in its annotation that it requires access to a secret for authentication purposes. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the whoami namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the whoami-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. The workload does not need any secret access at all, but the misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading all four files together — the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding grant it exactly that.

example_76.category: Unnecessary permissions for authenticated users on persistent volume claims
example_76.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, delete, and watch permissions on all persistent volume claims in the storage namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can manage all persistent volume claims in the storage namespace. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous verbs being granted, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_77.category: Unnecessary secret access for all authenticated users
example_77.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to system:unauthenticated, meaning any authenticated user can now read all secrets in the cluster. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together — the role alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_78.category: Unnecessary network policy access for authenticated users
example_78.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on all networkpolicies in the api namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can manage all network policies in the api namespace. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous verbs being granted, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being restricted.

example_79.category: Overly broad cluster role binding to authenticated users
example_79.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants bind permissions on all ClusterRoles. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the system:authenticated group, meaning any authenticated user can bind to this role and manage all ClusterRoles in the cluster. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_80.category: Unnecessary service account access for token creation
example_80.justification: The role.yaml grants create and get/list permissions on the /serviceaccounts/token resource. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can now create a token in the staging namespace. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together — the role alone does not reveal the sensitive permission being granted.

example_81.category: Unnecessary RBAC permissions for Grafana services and secrets access
example_81.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Grafana workload running grafana/grafana:10.0.0 with specific resource requests and limits for memory and CPU. The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, delete permissions on configmaps and services in the monitoring namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the grafana-sa ServiceAccount within the monitoring namespace only. However, Grafana itself needs access to secrets like the one used for authentication (e.g., a TLS secret) which is not restricted by any RBAC rules. This misconfiguration allows unauthorized users with the service account to potentially read and modify sensitive information without proper authorization.

example_82.category: Unnecessary RBAC permissions for a CI pipeline workload

The role.yaml grants get permissions on all secrets in the gateway namespace, including the api-gateway-tls secret required by the deployment. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the api-gateway-sa ServiceAccount which is mounted by the deployment. Reading all four files together reveals that the TLS certificate reader role has been granted access to a secret that is only needed for secure communication with the API gateway, and the binding restricts it to exactly that one secret. The misconfiguration becomes apparent when considering how this unnecessary access could be exploited.

example_75.category: Unnecessary secret access for a workload that does not require it
example_75.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a queue-worker workload running Python:3.11.0 and explicitly states in its annotation that it requires access to the rabbitmq-credentials secret for RabbitMQ credentials. However, the role.yaml grants get permissions on all secrets via resourceNames scoping. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the queue-worker-sa ServiceAccount which is mounted by the deployment. Reading all four files together reveals that the workload does not need the access granted — it only requires RabbitMQ credentials for its specific purpose and the binding restricts this access to exactly that one secret, but the permissions are unnecessarily broad.

example_116.category: Overly broad role binding to a service account in the monitoring namespace
example_116.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all pods. The rolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the monitoring-sa ServiceAccount within the monitoring namespace, meaning any user or service account in the monitoring namespace can now manage all pods across the entire cluster. This misconfiguration is only apparent when reading both files together: the role alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_117.category: Unnecessary role binding to a specific group for general access
example_117.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all configmaps in the logging namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the logging-team Group, which is not restricted to any particular resources or namespaces. This misconfiguration allows any user within the logging team to access all configmaps in the entire logging namespace without needing a specific resource or namespace scope.

example_118.category: Unnecessary cluster-level access for a specific user role
example_118.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on deployments in the cicd namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to a User named cicd-pipeline-operator within the same namespace only. This misconfiguration is visible by reading both files together: the user has been granted access to all deployments in the cicd namespace without any need for it, and the binding correctly restricts this access to exactly that one specific role.

example_119.category: Unnecessary secret access for sensitive data
example_119.justification: The role.yaml grants get permissions on all secrets in the database namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to a ServiceAccount named database-sa, which is mounted by a workload that does not need access to any sensitive data. This misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous resourceNames, and the binding file alone does not restrict access to the sensitive secrets.

example_120.category: Cluster role binding to a non-admin group
example_120.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on jobs in the ml namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the ml-team Group within the ml namespace, which is not an admin group but rather a team-specific group. This misconfiguration allows any user with access to the ml namespace to view all jobs created by the ml team, potentially exposing sensitive information or allowing unauthorized access.
